newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-Taylor's Rule and NZ monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Taylor's Rule and NZ monetary policy.

text.p: By Paul Stewart, Chief Economist at ANZ Banking Group (NZ) Ltd.

WELLINGTON, Sept 13 - I am sure central bankers would like to think that the process of controlling inflation involves much more science than art, but the reality is that policy makers rely upon personal judgement (gut feel) and a bit of luck more than they would ideally like.
Nonetheless, considerable effort does go into developing an objective framework which determines what monetary policy settings are appropriate at any point in time.
A recent issue of The Economist contained an article about one such attempt, the rule developed in 1993 by John Taylor, an economist at Stanford University.

Taylor, currently an adviser to Bob Dole, argued that central banks should "lean against the wind" when setting interest rates and provide a method to calculate the appropriate level of short term interest rates given the prevailing inflation and growth conditions.

The Economist noted that both Taylor's work and subsequent research suggestED that the central banks in the U.S., Germany and Japan have (whether by accident or design) effectively been following the rule for some time.
So what about New Zealand?

Taylor's rule says that short term interest rates (say 90 day bank bills) should be equal to: the real short term interest rate (i.e. actual interest rate less inflation) which is consistent with "neutral" monetary policy; plus the expected inflation rate; plus (minus) 0.5 percent for every percent that current inflation is above (below) its target; plus (minus) 0.5
percent for every percent that current GDP growth is above (below) the potential GDP growth rate.

As a starting point for New Zealand, we adopted five percent as the neutral real short term interest rate, three percent as the potential growth rate and the RBNZ's underlying inflation forecast 12 months forward as the expected inflation rate.
On that basis, what does Taylor's rule tell us about monetary policy in the 1990s?
Firstly, it suggests that in the late 1993/early 1994 monetary policy was too loose.
In retrospect, most would agree that to be a fair assessment because with the economy strengthening, the RBNZ's inflation forecasts at that point were overly optimistic.
Secondly, it suggests that monetary policy is currently overly restrictive. According to the rule, short term interest rates should be around 2.5-3.0 percent lower than they are at present.
However, thirdly, it suggests that apart from the brief period in 1993-94, monetary policy has been too tight for all of the last six years.
And that is where the rule (or our application of it) starts to go wrong!

If monetary policy has been consistently too tight, then clearly underlying inflation should have been less than one percent (the mid-point of the target), possibly even below zero percent for most of that period.

The fact that underlying inflation has never been below one percent and has spent a considerable amount of time near the top of, or above, the inflation target, implies that monetary policy has, if anything, been too loose.
So what is wrong with the rule and why doesn't it apply to New Zealand? An important issue is that Taylor's rule focuses exclusively upon interest rates.

That may be reasonably appropriate for the U.S., but in a small trade-dependent economy where the exposure to imported inflation is much higher, a measure which does not explicitly capture the impact of the exchange rate on monetary conditions will be incomplete.
Another possibility is that we have applied the rule incorrectly. Specifically, we have rather subjectively set the "neutral" real short term interest rate at five percent.
We could use the average historical short term rate. For the U.S. and U.K., that is around two percent and 3.5 percent respectively.
Indeed, applying New Zealand's average for the last six years (around 6.5 percent) does improve the fit of the rule to actual rates.

However, in another research paper cited by The Economist, Alison Stuart of the Bank of England notes that "theoretically" the neutral real short term rate should be close to the long run trend rate of economic growth.
That would imply a much lower rate for New Zealand (3.0-3.5 percent), which would then reduce the performance of the Taylor rule further.
Taylor's rule seems to add little in the New Zealand context (and I would argue has limited use for any economy).

The fact is that the process of controlling inflation and setting monetary policy is not a simple mechanical process based on exact information. Economic relationships are complex and contingent upon the human factor, changeable through time.

The difficulty faced by central bankers in rigorously analysing large amounts of sketchy and often lagged information as a basis for setting policy, which will have an imprecise impact upwards of a year into the future, should not be underestimated.
However, this exercise has reinforced one important point. That is, real short term interest rates in New Zealand have remained persistently high compared to other industrialised economies.
Why is that? Essentially, despite modest inflation expectations (generally measured at 2.0-3.0 percent), household and business behaviour is not yet consistent with a low inflation environment.
New Zealanders appear to have a very high propensity to borrow (especially for property investment) and are reluctant to save even with high real interest rates.
Until that changes, the Reserve Bank will have to "lean a little more heavily against the wind" than the Taylor rule advocates.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
